summary: This document describes the problem of caller ID impersonation in VoIP systems interworking with the telephone network. Attackers can fake calling numbers for bulk calling schemes or fraud, and it lays out requirements for a way to authenticate the identity of callers.

eli5.summary: Anyone can write any name on a letter's return address. This RFC explains why that is a problem for phone calls and what we need so you can trust who is really calling.

questions: how to stop caller id spoofing
why does sip identity not work for phone numbers
subtitle: Why caller ID on VoIP and phone networks is so easy to fake, and what a fix would have to do.

tldr.problem: Interworking VoIP with the traditional telephone network gave attackers cheap tools to impersonate or hide calling numbers for bulk calling schemes, voicemail hacking and fraud. Earlier fixes (P-Asserted-Identity and SIP Identity) never worked well enough at scale.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines why earlier attempts failed, lists what has changed since, and sets out high-level requirements: in-band identity that survives gateways and B2BUAs, credentials rooted in existing national number delegations, and minimal overhead.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement and requirements document, not a protocol. It starts the STIR work and leaves security considerations for specific solutions to later documents.

today: RFC 7340 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a problem statement and set of requirements rather than a protocol, and the RFC leaves security considerations for specific solutions to later documents.

sections.title: The Caller ID Problem
sections.content:
RFC 7340 explains why identifying the calling party for telephone numbers on the Internet has proven so difficult. Over the past decade, Voice over IP (VoIP) systems based on SIP replaced many traditional telephony deployments. Connecting them to the traditional telephone network (the PSTN) lowered the assurance of calling party numbers and Caller ID.

The RFC says that attackers can now impersonate or obscure numbers to run bulk commercial calling schemes, hack voicemail boxes, or even get around multi-factor authentication systems trusted by banks. Number spoofing is used in two ways: impersonation (pretending to be a specific person) and anonymization (switching between numbers so the caller cannot be traced or blocked).

The RFC also notes that simply outlawing spoofing is not enough, because those who spoof numbers are already committing other crimes. Some spoofing is legitimate, such as a doctor's office showing the office number or a call center showing a company's number.
sections.eli5: It is like a prank caller who can write any phone number they like on the caller screen. Some people do it to steal things, so we need a way to check the number is real.

sections.title: Key Terms and Call Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC defines four terms. In-band identity conveyance puts call origin information in the protocol that sets up the call. Out-of-band identity verification checks whether the number exists, whether the caller may use it, and whether a call was recently made from it. The authority delegation infrastructure covers who holds authority over numbers as they are ported and delegated, and a canonical telephone number form lets both approaches compare numbers.

Section 4 walks through six call paths: VoIP-to-VoIP, VoIP-PSTN-VoIP, PSTN-to-VoIP, VoIP-to-PSTN, PSTN-VoIP-PSTN and PSTN-to-PSTN. It assumes the PSTN part of any call path cannot be altered. In each mixed case a gateway creates or re-creates the signaling, so the question is whether it can be trusted to state or check the number. For PSTN-to-PSTN calls, the RFC suggests out-of-band IP connectivity at both carriers might be used to validate the call information.
sections.eli5: A phone call can travel through the old phone system, the Internet, or both, like a parcel passing between different delivery companies. Each hand-off is a chance for the sender's name to get lost or changed.

sections.title: Why Existing Solutions Fall Short
sections.content:
P-Asserted-Identity (RFC 3325) lets trusted network entities share an authoritative identifier for the caller. It is simple and widely deployed, but it needs a trust domain, offers no cryptographic validation, and all trust is transitive: its assurance is only as good as the least trustworthy member of the domain. The RFC also says the "P-" header approach has been deprecated (see RFC 5727).

SIP Identity (RFC 4474) adds a signature over the From header and other parts of the request. The RFC names two fundamental limitations that stopped deployment: it provides identity only for domain names rather than telephone numbers, and it does not tolerate intermediaries that alter bodies or certain header fields, such as B2BUAs and PSTN gateways.

VIPR (Verification Involving PSTN Reachability) discovers who answers a number by calling it on the PSTN and then sets up an out-of-band connection. It only helps for repeated communication, so it has no answer to the classic robocall from a number that has never called before, and its public distributed hash table creates a new attack surface and privacy loss. The RFC concludes that SIP Identity and VIPR have had little impact in the marketplace.
sections.eli5: Earlier fixes were like a school ID that only works inside one building, a stamp that breaks when someone repacks the box, and a secret handshake that only works the second time you meet. None solved the real problem.

sections.title: What Has Changed Since
sections.content:
Section 6 lists changes in the environment that may open new strategies. The rise of smartphones, which have both a PSTN and an IP interface, suggests that out-of-band rendezvous could be adapted, possibly with a trusted centralized database. Public ENUM has little prospect of adoption as originally envisioned, but some national authorities are moving number provisioning to the Internet and issuing credentials that express authority for numbers.

Web certificate authority compromises are a lesson: the RFC says to be wary of excessive pluralism, and that a chain of delegation with narrowing authority is needed but there is no need for multiple roots claiming the same number or range. B2BUAs are common, so the elements that are signed could be reviewed.

Some things stay the same. Trust in the PSTN remains transitive, so a gateway has little chance of knowing whether a caller was authorized to claim a number, and that case may prove beyond repair. The RFC also warns that identity information attached to calls could feed pervasive monitoring, and says the work is not meant to eliminate anonymity.
sections.eli5: Things changed: almost everyone now has a smartphone, and we have learned lessons about who to trust to hand out certificates. That gives us new ideas, though the old phone network still cannot be fully trusted.

sections.title: Basic Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC lists high-level requirements for what became the STIR effort. Intermediaries as well as end systems must be able to generate and validate source identity information, and validation must work without human intervention. A solution must survive the transition of the call to the PSTN and the presence of B2BUAs.

Credentials must be staged on existing national-level number delegations, without assuming an international golden root on the Internet. It must allow number portability among carriers and support legitimate number spoofing such as doctors' offices and call centers. It must cause minimal expansion of SIP header fields to avoid fragmentation when UDP is used, minimize round trips and cryptographic operations, and limit what an unauthorized party can learn about who called whom.

Out of scope are validating the caller's display name and authenticating responses (requests only). The security considerations section says that those for specific solutions will be discussed in solution documents.
sections.eli5: The rules for a good fix: it must work for everyone, check itself automatically, still let a doctor show the office number, stay small, and not tell strangers who is calling whom.

viz.caption: THE THREE EARLIER APPROACHES AS DESCRIBED IN RFC 7340

cells: Trusted entities in a trust domain share the caller identity
Signature over the From header and other parts of the request
Domain names only; breaks with intermediaries that alter requests
Call the number on the PSTN, then connect out of band
Helps only repeated contacts; public DHT
